title: Hanukkah: the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 4)
hookLine: the revolt against Antiochus and the Temple rededicated, told in the books of Maccabees

lines: A STORY THAT STARTS WITH GRIEF.
cards: A small band of fighters walks up to the Temple in Jerusalem, and stops. The gates are burned. The priests' rooms are torn down.
Weeds have grown up in the courtyards, the text says, like a forest or a hillside. The altar has been used for offerings their law forbids. These men have just won battles against a much larger army.
And the first thing they do, standing in the ruin, is tear their clothes and put ashes on their heads, the way you'd mourn a death. The story of Hanukkah, in this telling, starts with grief.

teach.h: A BOOK OUTSIDE THE JEWISH BIBLE.
teach.b: The account here is the First Book of Maccabees. It isn't in the Jewish Bible; it was preserved in Greek, and it's part of the Catholic and Orthodox Christian Bibles.
The Greek king Antiochus the Fourth ruled the land. He banned Torah study, circumcision and Shabbat, and set up a pagan altar in the Temple. Some Jews went along; others resisted.
In the village of Modiin, an old priest named Mattathias refused to offer a pagan sacrifice and fled to the hills with his five sons. One son, Judah, nicknamed the Maccabee, led a guerrilla army.
Before one battle, as the book tells it, his men were afraid of the size of the enemy.
Judah answered that victory doesn't depend on numbers; strength comes from heaven. Chapter four is the homecoming. They pull down the defiled altar, and then don't know what to do with its stones.
So they store them on the Temple mount, the text says, until a prophet should come and tell them.

They build a new altar of whole stones, light the lampstand, and on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev dedicate it, with songs and harps and cymbals, for eight days. Judah decrees the days be kept every year.
Later, the prayer added on Hanukkah thanks God for delivering the many into the hands of the few.

how: Hanukkah is kept for eight nights from the twenty-fifth of Kislev, with candles lit each night and the Al HaNissim prayer added to the daily prayers and grace after meals, recalling the Hasmonean victory and the rededication.

a harvest festival for gathering the olives
dedication: the Temple's altar rebuilt, eight days

games.q: you've pulled down the defiled altar. its stones were once holy, then used for forbidden offerings. what do you do with them?
o: reuse them for the new altar.
store them away until a prophet can decide.
games.why: they laid the stones up on the mount, until a prophet should come and tell them what to do. some questions, they decided, could wait.

practice: Name one thing you care about that feels outnumbered in your life right now: honesty at work, rest in a busy house, a practice nobody around you shares.
Hold it the way the Maccabees held those altar stones, carefully, without rushing to decide everything. Breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Hanukkah. Dedication: the altar rebuilt and the Temple rededicated, for eight days, in the month of Kislev. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: dedication, the same root as the dedication of an altar or a house.
